PAGALING KA, MUNING!  🐈
Sa gitna ng nagpapatuloy na malawakang sunog sa Parola, Binondo, Manila, isang babae ang lumapit sa Manila Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Department EMS team habang karga ang kaniyang alagang pusa na nagtamo ng mga paso sa iba’t ibang bahagi ng katawan.

Bagama’t walang inaasikasong pasyenteng tao nang mga oras na iyon, agad namang rumesponde ang Manila DRRM EMS team upang bigyan ng paunang lunas si “Muning.”

Maingat nilang nilinis at inirigahan ang mga paso, nilagyan ng burn cream, at binalutan ng gasa ang mga sugat ng pusa upang maiwasan ang impeksiyon at mapabilis ang paggaling nito.

Courtesy: Manila Public Information Office/Facebook

Bisitahin ang https://t.co/bAMF9JO2Xs para sa updates.

Sankei exclusively reports that Tokyo internally assessed during the 2010 Defense Guidelines Review that, in the event of Chinese unification with Taiwan, securing critical SLOC around Japan could become effectively “impossible”: https://t.co/RdS03hayCY.

■Translation
Exclusive:  JMOD Assessed Impact of Chinese Unification with Taiwan During 2010 Defense Guidelines Review — Sea Lane Security Deemed “Impossible”

It was revealed on May 23 that Japan’s Ministry of Defense had previously examined the military implications for Japan of a Chinese unification with Taiwan. The issue was discussed internally during the drafting of the 2010 National Defense Program Guidelines (NDPG). The discussions coincided with a period in which the Chinese military was modernizing through measures such as acquiring aircraft carriers and intensifying activities around Japan, indicating that the ministry had already been considering scenarios involving a further deterioration of the security environment.

Sources familiar with the matter disclosed the details. At the time, discussions examined the effects that would arise if the Chinese military gained access to Taiwan’s ports and airports, including impacts on:

air superiority;
the security of maritime lines of communication; and
the foundations for U.S. military reinforcement operations.

The discussions concluded that China’s operational reach and available military capabilities would significantly expand, while its anti-access/area denial (A2/AD) capabilities aimed at keeping U.S. forces at bay would dramatically improve. It was further concluded that the military balance around Japan would fundamentally change, forcing a reassessment of the Self-Defense Forces’ posture and defense concepts.

Regarding air superiority, the assessment estimated that China would be able to redirect forces currently oriented toward Taiwan against Japan, while also deploying shorter-range aircraft that previously could not effectively operate in the area. As a result, Chinese air power would be substantially strengthened in practical terms. Concerns were raised that, under the SDF posture at the time, securing air superiority around the Southwest Islands would become “impossible.”

In terms of maritime traffic, concerns were raised that if the Chinese military became able to use Su’ao Port in Yilan County in northeastern Taiwan, China would gain a sortie base outside the First Island Chain (stretching from off Kyushu through Okinawa, Taiwan, and the Philippines). The assessment projected that securing maritime traffic safety in the southwestern direction would become “impossible,” while the southeastern direction would face “serious disruption.” It also suggested that Japan’s existing sea lane defense concept would become difficult to sustain.

In the event of an invasion of Japan, Japan would receive reinforcement from U.S. forces under the U.S.-Japan alliance. However, the assessment concluded that if China used Taiwan as a foothold, securing the maritime traffic necessary to support U.S. reinforcement operations would become “difficult.” This highlighted the need for Japan to develop the capacity to endure for an extended period on its own.

Although such scenarios were not formally incorporated into the 2010 NDPG drafted under the Democratic Party of Japan administration, the findings are believed to have contributed to the second Shinzo Abe administration, established in 2012, shifting toward strengthening Japan’s defense capabilities.

China’s defense budget stood at approximately 500 billion yuan in FY2010, but has increased to roughly 1.9 trillion yuan in FY2026. Japan’s security environment has deteriorated significantly compared to the situation in 2010.
